what_it_does: Finding which stored item is most similar to a query — for instance, finding the closest image in a database to a new photo — often relies on measuring the angle between two long lists of numbers (called vectors), a calculation known as cosine similarity. Doing this for millions of stored vectors is power-hungry because all those numbers have to be loaded and compared. This paper proposes Seg-Cos, a system that performs this search inside specialized memory chips called TCAMs (ternary content-addressable memories), which can compare many patterns simultaneously without moving data to a processor. The key idea is to break each high-dimensional vector into smaller segments and encode each segment as a range of angles, so the TCAM can check many candidates in parallel. Extra tricks — grouping nearby computations together and combining small lookup results into higher-precision answers — reduce the number of memory rows that need to be activated, cutting energy use. The overall effect is that similarity search for tasks like few-shot learning and nearest-neighbor lookup can be done more efficiently in hardware.
